questions.q: How fast was Vikram moving sideways when its powered descent began 30 km above the Moon?
questions.do: In Land Vikram yourself, click Fly all 30 km and read the Sideways tile before you press Start.
questions.a: About 1,688 m/s (about 1.69 km/s). That is the speed of its 25 × 134 km orbit. The engines had to remove almost all of it to land.

questions.q: When the autopilot flies ISRO’s plan, how long does the whole powered descent take, and how much propellant is left at touchdown?
questions.do: Click Watch ISRO’s plan, then Start descent and wait for touchdown. You can also read the last row of the table in Did the replay find the Moon?
questions.a: About 19 minutes, with only about 13 kg of propellant left out of 950 kg. The page calls it “tight, as it was for ISRO”.

questions.q: Compare the start of the descent with the 150 m hover. How do Full thrust ÷ weight and Propellant change? Why?
questions.do: Click Fly all 30 km and read Full thrust ÷ weight and Propellant. Then click Take over at the 150 m hover and read them again.
questions.a: At 30 km: about 1.16 and 950 kg. At the hover: about 2.35 and 35 kg. The engines are the same, but the lander has burned most of its propellant, so it is much lighter and the same thrust lifts it more easily.

questions.q: Apollo 11 reached the Moon in three days. Chandrayaan-3 took forty. Did the long route need more push? Why did ISRO take it?
questions.do: Read the box Why forty days, not three? and compare its two push numbers.
questions.a: No. One single burn would need about 662 m/s; ISRO’s six burns add up to about 663 m/s, nearly the same. The long way saves a bigger rocket: LVM3 could only leave the craft in a stretched orbit, and its small engine works best in short pushes at the low point of each orbit.

questions.q: What went wrong with Chandrayaan-2’s lander in 2019, and what is this lab’s pass mark for a safe touchdown?
questions.do: Read the paragraph at the top of Land Vikram yourself and the note under the controls.
questions.a: Chandrayaan-2’s lander was still falling at 58 m/s at 330 m and crashed. The pass mark here is slower than 3 m/s downward and 1 m/s sideways. On 23 August 2023 Chandrayaan-3 made India the fourth country to land softly on the Moon.
